title: Recognizing Conflict Markers
subtopics: Distinguishing base, current, and incoming changes
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose and boundaries of recognizing conflict markers.
Choose and interpret a Git command relevant to recognizing conflict markers using a disposable repository.
Verify the result with repository state or history and identify one safety limitation.

content.intro: This lesson introduces recognizing conflict markers as part of Merging and Resolving Conflicts. It follows the supplied Git curriculum and adds an original explanation, an inspectable command example, troubleshooting notes, and a practice task.
content.why_it_matters: Conflict markers delimit sections that Git could not automatically combine. The developer must inspect both sides and any shared context, edit the desired final content, and remove the markers before staging the resolution.

content_blocks.title: Resolve a merge conflict deliberately
content_blocks.alt_text: A conflict asks the developer to decide the final content. Inspect both sides, edit the file, stage the resolution, and verify before completing the merge.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text:
**Core idea.** Conflict markers delimit sections that Git could not automatically combine. The developer must inspect both sides and any shared context, edit the desired final content, and remove the markers before staging the resolution.

For **Recognizing Conflict Markers**, keep the named subtopics in view: Opening conflicted files; Understanding conflict-marker sections; Distinguishing base, current, and incoming changes; Identifying the intended final content. Treat those as the scope of this lesson, then practise the smallest workflow that demonstrates the idea.

content_blocks.title: How to reason about it
content_blocks.text: **Before you run a command:** decide what state you are inspecting or changing, identify whether the effect is local or remote, and write down what evidence would count as success. Open each conflicted text file and inspect the conflict markers. The command identifies paths; it does not decide which content is correct.

content_blocks.title: Safety and verification checkpoint
content_blocks.text: Start with git status --short --branch. For destructive or history-rewriting operations, review the exact target, create a recovery reference when appropriate, and keep valuable work backed up. Never put credentials, access tokens or private keys in course submissions.

common_mistakes.problem: Running a state-changing command without confirming the target repository or branch.
common_mistakes.why: A command may affect the wrong working tree or move a reference that other work depends on.
common_mistakes.fix: Check git rev-parse --show-toplevel and git status --short --branch before proceeding.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming a command succeeded because no error was visible.
common_mistakes.why: Some Git commands are silent on success, and some expected actions are blocked by repository state or permissions.
common_mistakes.fix: Verify status, log, references, remote state or the named output explicitly.

common_mistakes.problem: Using an example placeholder literally or applying a destructive example to valuable work.
common_mistakes.why: Paths, branch names and object IDs depend on the current repository; restore/reset/clean operations can discard work.
common_mistakes.fix: Substitute real practice values, use a disposable repository, and preview changes before proceeding.
